deep.reconstruction:
This page continues E598, Euler's exposition of Lagrange's reduction theory for the prime divisors of binary quadratic forms. The general method is set up on the preceding pages (Problems 3 and 4). A divisor D of p^2 ± n q^2, with gcd(p,q)=1, is written as f r^2 + 2g rs + h s^2 with fh − g^2 = ±n and the reduced bound g < √(n/3). Euler then tests which residues a mod 4n such divisors can have.

(1) End of Example 5, n=3. The previous page left the case g=1, f=h=2, giving D = r^2+rs+s^2. If s is even, s=2t, this is (r+t)^2+3t^2. If s is odd, Euler takes r odd too (otherwise he falls back on the even case) and sets r = 2t−s. Then D = 4t^2 − 2ts + s^2 = 3t^2 + (t−s)^2. So every divisor is again of the form r^2+3s^2. The admissible residues mod 12 come from a = p^2 ≡ 1 and a = p^2+3 ≡ 7 (p even). Hence divisors lie in 12i+1 or 12i+7, equivalently 12i+1, −5. The excluded classes are 12i+5 and 12i+11, i.e. 12i−1, +5. Euler notes a general rule for the forms p^2+nq^2: the excluded residues are the negatives of the admitted ones. In modern terms the character (−4n/·) is odd.

(2) Example 6: p^2−3q^2, also written 3p^2−q^2. With n=3 only g=0 occurs, fh=3, so D = r^2−3s^2, read up to sign, i.e. including 3r^2−s^2. Hence divisors have the same form. The residues mod 12 come from a = p^2 ≡ 1 and a = 3−p^2 ≡ −1, so divisors are 12i±1 and 12i±5 is excluded.

(3) Scholion §24. Euler recalls that he had long ago handled these cases and shown that the divisors have the same form. This fails for larger n. Square-divisible n are excluded, since p^2 ± k m^2 q^2 reduces to p^2 ± k q'^2.

(4) Example 7: p^2+5q^2. Since g < √(5/3), g = 0 or 1. The case g=0 gives fh=5 and r^2+5s^2. The case g=1 gives fh=6, i.e. r^2+2rs+6s^2 = (r+s)^2+5s^2, or the genuinely new form 2r^2+2rs+3s^2. For the latter 2D = (2r+s)^2+5s^2. So every divisor is either of the form p^2+5q^2 or has its double of that form. This is class number 2 for discriminant −20. The residues mod 20 begin with 1 and 9 from a = p^2; the next page adds 3 and 7 from (p^2+5)/2.
errors: Example 6 states D = rr−3ss, but x^2−3y^2 and −(x^2−3y^2) = 3y^2−x^2 are inequivalent forms, since the fundamental unit 2+√3 has norm +1. For example 11 is represented only by 3p^2−q^2 (11 = 3·4−1), not by p^2−3q^2. Primes ≡ 1 mod 12 are p^2−3q^2 and primes ≡ 11 mod 12 are 3p^2−q^2. Euler's title ('pp−3qq etiam 3pp−qq') covers this, but the solution suppresses the sign distinction.
Example 6 says 'alii valores non prodeunt praeter a=1', yet a = 3−p^2 with p even gives a ≡ −1 mod 12. Euler's conclusion 12i±1 is right; the wording is loose.
Example 5's parity argument ('r must be odd, otherwise we return to the previous case') is terse. The case r even, s odd is handled by symmetry, swapping r and s. This is a gap in exposition only.

ideas.what: Reduction of r^2+rs+s^2 to the form x^2+3y^2 by a parity argument
ideas.modern_name: Equivalence of the forms (1,1,1) and (1,0,3) as representers of the same primes; class number one for discriminants −3 and −12
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (for p = x^2+3y^2) and Lagrange (reduction theory)
ideas.where_published: Euler's earlier papers on divisors of x^2+3y^2 (E256/E272 era); Lagrange, Recherches d'arithmétique (1773–75)

ideas.what: Admissible residue classes of prime divisors mod 4n (12i+1, 7; 12i±1; 20i+1, 3, 7, 9), with the excluded classes being the negatives of the admitted ones when n>0
ideas.modern_name: Genus/character theory: the quadratic character (−4n/·) is odd for positive n and even for p^2−nq^2
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (empirical tables of divisors), Lagrange, Legendre, Gauss
ideas.where_published: E164 'Theoremata circa divisores numerorum in hac forma pa^2 ± qb^2 contentorum'; Euler–Goldbach correspondence

ideas.modern_name: Restriction to squarefree n / fundamental discriminants

ideas.what: For p^2+5q^2, the two reduced forms x^2+5y^2 and 2x^2+2xy+3y^2: every divisor D is of the form or has 2D of the form
ideas.modern_name: Class number h(−20) = 2; the composition-type relation 2·(2,2,3) ~ (1,0,5)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (conjecture, 1744 Goldbach letter); Lagrange (proof via reduction)
ideas.where_published: Euler–Goldbach correspondence 1744; E164; Lagrange 1773–75; discussed in Cox, 'Primes of the form x^2+ny^2'

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a routine application of Lagrange's reduction theory, which this very paper popularizes, to n = 3, −3 and 5. All results are well documented: h(−20) = 2, the residue classes, and Euler's earlier conjectures on these forms. Nothing new for a specialist.
transcription_corrections: Example 6 is numbered '§. 23' in the print (the image confirms it). Example 5 on the previous page also has §.23, so this is an original misnumbering; the Scholion that follows is §.24.
'g<√3' in Example 6 is presumably Euler's bound √(n/3) = 1 for n=3, giving g=0; the printed radical is ambiguous in the scan.
The garbled closing phrase 'valores ipsius a negatiuos esse ipsius a' should mean that the excluded values are the negatives of the admitted values of a, as in the parallel remark on p. 290.
